question: Which of the following statements about events, incidents and breaches is correct?
option_a: All events are incidents, but only some incidents are events
option_b: All incidents are events, but not all events are incidents, and only some incidents become breaches
option_c: An event and an incident are the same thing viewed at different times
option_d: A breach is any observable occurrence, most of them benign

question: Which option lists the four phases of the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle in the correct order?
option_a: Detection & Analysis; Preparation; Post-Incident Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery
option_b: Preparation; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Detection & Analysis; Post-Incident Analysis
option_c: Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Analysis

question: In one or two sentences: during containment, why may blocking a user at the identity provider not be enough, and what else may be required?
accepted_answers: a blocked user may still hold a valid session token; federated identity separates authentication from authorisation; actions may be needed on both the identity provider and the relying party; revoke sessions at the relying party as well

question: An organisation states that it can afford to lose at most one hour of recent data for its ordering system. Which target has it set?
In one or two sentences: what is compliance inheritance, and which part of the compliance task remains the customer's own?
accepted_answers: the customer inherits the provider's control set for the infrastructure layer; compliance of whatever the customer builds on top remains the customer's own task; inherit the provider's compliance for its layers; stay responsible for your own software; shared-responsibility model in the language of audit

question: According to Comer, why do side channels and back doors belong in the risk register?
option_a: They are stopped by a correctly configured firewall, so the register records the firewall rule
option_b: They are structural risks that no firewall or password stops, so the register exists to record and accept them knowingly
option_c: They only occur in on-premises data centres, so cloud tenants can ignore them
option_d: They are examples of compliance inheritance from the provider

question: Building on the chapter exercise "Why rebuild rather than patch": the timeline for the Nextcloud incident in the chapter's example shows that the attacker held an administrator credential for two days and pushed at least one change to a container image. A colleague proposes to patch the running container, re-enable the admin account with a new password, and close the incident. Walk through Containment, Eradication & Recovery as this chapter describes them for the cloud, explain what the colleague's plan misses, and name the control from an earlier session that each of your steps relies on.
sample_answer: Containment: disable the account and revoke its sessions (federated identity means a valid token may outlive the block) and isolate the workload; IAM and the management plane are top priorities (Session 7). Eradication: rotate all credentials, enforce MFA and policy conditions (Session 7); delete the tampered image and old images, function code and IaC, because a careless redeployment could let the attacker back in (Session 5). Recovery: redeploy hardened versions from IaC after analysing images and templates for backdoors, and restore from the clean, tested backup (Session 11); capture incident data under chain of custody (Session 10). The colleague's plan leaves backdoors in the image, ignores other stolen credentials and live tokens, skips MFA, and closes without Post-Incident Analysis feeding lessons back into preparation.
